triage.name: Delirium
triage.reason: Acute confusional state with fluctuating course; core hospital diagnosis reached by history, exam and workup for toxic, metabolic and infectious causes.

review_issues: auto-repaired: workup: 'Chest x-ray' was in initial, not_indicated; kept initial as a conditional order (only if pneumonia is suspected (fever, hypoxia, cough, or focal lung findings))

auto-repaired: workup: 'CT head without contrast' was in supporting, not_indicated; kept supporting as a conditional order (only if focal neurologic deficit, recent fall, anticoagulation, or acute severe headache)

auto-repaired: workup: 'MRI brain without contrast' was in supporting, not_indicated; kept supporting as a conditional order (only if CT negative but high suspicion for stroke, encephalitis, or seizure)
auto-repaired: workup: 'EEG' was in supporting, not_indicated; kept supporting as a conditional order (only if possible nonconvulsive seizure or unexplained fluctuating level of consciousness)
auto-repaired: workup: 'Lumbar puncture' was in supporting, not_indicated; kept supporting as a conditional order (only if fever, headache, nuchal rigidity, or suspected CNS infection)
auto-repaired: workup: 'ABG' was in supporting, not_indicated; kept supporting as a conditional order (only if hypoxia or acid-base disturbance suspected)
auto-repaired: workup: 'Urine drug screen' was in supporting, not_indicated; kept supporting as a conditional order (only if substance use suspected or unexplained delirium)
auto-repaired: workup: 'Blood alcohol level' was in supporting, not_indicated; kept supporting as a conditional order (only if alcohol use suspected or withdrawal)
auto-repaired: workup: 'ECG' was in supporting, not_indicated; kept supporting as a conditional order (only if cardiac ischemia, arrhythmia, or drug toxicity suspected)

demographics: Most common in older adults, especially those who are hospitalized, institutionalized, or have pre-existing cognitive impairment
Occurs with similar frequency in men and women
Risk rises with age, severity of acute illness, and number of predisposing factors

risk_factors.text: Severe acute illness or multiple comorbidities
Hospitalization or intensive care unit stay
Surgery, especially hip fracture or cardiac surgery
Use of psychoactive medications or polypharmacy
Sensory impairment such as poor vision or hearing
Immobility or use of physical restraints

social_history: Living in a nursing home or prolonged hospitalization

chief_complaints.text: I feel confused and I can't think clearly
I don't know where I am or what day it is
I saw things that weren't there

hpi.onset: Acute, over hours to a few days; symptoms often fluctuate from hour to hour and tend to be worse at night.
hpi.duration: Hours to days at presentation; may persist for days to weeks while the underlying cause is treated.
hpi.progression: Begins as trouble paying attention and sleep-wake reversal, then progresses to disorientation, incoherent thoughts, and sometimes hallucinations or agitation. Symptoms wax and wane, with lucid intervals.
hpi.quality: Clouded sensorium with trouble focusing; thoughts may be fragmented or rambling.
hpi.severity: Variable; from mild inattention and restlessness to severe agitation or unresponsive sleepiness.
hpi.timing: Fluctuating; commonly worse in the evening and overnight.

associated_symptoms.text: Trouble keeping my mind on one thing or following what is said
Not knowing the date, place, or who people are
Day and night are reversed: sleepy during the day, awake at night
Seeing or hearing things that are not there
Believing that people are trying to harm me
Feeling restless and picking at the sheets or tubes
Very sleepy and hard to wake

pertinent_negatives: Gradual memory loss over months to years
Normal attention on repeated bedside testing
Clear consciousness with hallucinations or delusions

argues_against: Hallucinations with clear sensorium and intact attention
Well-systematized delusions with a normal level of consciousness

atypical.how_it_differs: Delirium may appear as irritability, inconsolable crying, refusal to interact, or emergence agitation after anesthesia. Young children cannot describe confusion or hallucinations, and disorientation may not be obvious.
Hypoactive delirium is more common and is often mistaken for depression or worsening dementia. Older adults may show lethargy, withdrawal, and poor oral intake rather than agitation.

general.mild: Alert but distractible; may appear mildly restless or lethargic
general.moderate: Fluctuating; sometimes sleepy and withdrawn, at other times agitated; may pick at bedclothes
general.severe: Marked agitation with shouting and pulling at tubes, or profound somnolence requiring repeated stimulation
general.critical: Stuporous or comatose, or severe hyperactive/autonomic overactivity; airway protection may be lost

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to recite the months backward or subtract serial sevens
findings.finding: Cannot stay focused; loses track of the task and gives up or makes errors

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient's name, place, and date
findings.finding: Disoriented to time and place, sometimes person

findings.maneuver: Observe level of arousal and coherence of speech
findings.finding: Clouded sensorium with rambling or incoherent speech

findings.maneuver: Observe motor behavior and attempts to remove devices
findings.finding: Restless, picking at bedclothes, trying to get out of bed

findings.maneuver: Attempt to rouse the patient with voice and light touch
findings.finding: Somnolent; falls asleep during the exam unless repeatedly stimulated

findings.maneuver: Have the patient hold arms outstretched with fingers spread
Ask the patient to extend arms and dorsiflex wrists, as if stopping traffic
findings.finding: Asterixis: brief downward flapping of hands

findings.maneuver: Test motor strength in all four limbs and face

findings.finding: No nuchal rigidity or resistance to flexion

labs.caveat: Leukocytosis suggests infection but is absent in many cases, especially viral or in older adults.
Hypoglycemia is a must-not-miss reversible cause; hyperglycemia also occurs with infection/diabetes but is less directly causal.
Sodium derangement in either direction can cause delirium; hyponatremia is more commonly the culprit.
Uremia from renal failure or dehydration can precipitate delirium.
Acute kidney injury may present with delirium.
Hypercalcemia is a classic metabolic cause; hypocalcemia can also alter mental status.
Hepatic encephalopathy; levels correlate poorly with severity but a high level in the right setting is diagnostic.
Elevated in hepatic injury; part of hepatic panel.
Elevated in hepatic failure or cholestasis.
Nonspecific marker of infection or inflammation.
Elevated in sepsis, hypoperfusion, or seizure.
Hypoxemia is a common precipitant; pulse oximetry may be normal with carbon monoxide or severe anemia.
Hypercapnia can cause confusion, especially in lung disease or oversedation.
Sterile pyuria can occur from an inflamed adjacent organ; but in older adults, UTI is a classic precipitant.

imaging.preferred_when: Emergency setting to rule out acute hemorrhage, stroke, or mass; CT is quicker than MRI
When CT is negative but high suspicion for stroke, encephalitis, or seizure
When pneumonia is suspected (fever, hypoxia, cough, or focal lung findings)

initial.why: Leukocytosis or anemia may point to infection or another precipitant
Identifies electrolyte, glucose, and renal contributors
Urinary tract infection is a common precipitant, especially in older adults

initial.only_if: pneumonia is suspected (fever, hypoxia, cough, or focal lung findings)

supporting.why: Liver tests may reveal hepatic encephalopathy

supporting.only_if: cirrhosis, liver failure, or unexplained delirium with flapping tremor

supporting.why: Screens for thyroid dysfunction as a metabolic cause
supporting.only_if: no obvious cause, older adult, or history of thyroid disease
urinalysis suggests infection or patient has urinary symptoms

supporting.why: Rules out stroke, hemorrhage, or mass
supporting.only_if: focal neurologic deficit, recent fall, anticoagulation, or acute severe headache

supporting.why: More sensitive for early ischemia and inflammatory lesions
supporting.only_if: CT negative but high suspicion for stroke, encephalitis, or seizure
possible nonconvulsive seizure or unexplained fluctuating level of consciousness
fever, headache, nuchal rigidity, or suspected CNS infection
substance use suspected or unexplained delirium

supporting.why: Looks for cardiac ischemia, arrhythmia, or drug toxicity
supporting.only_if: cardiac ischemia, arrhythmia, or drug toxicity suspected

not_indicated.why: No role in routine delirium evaluation
Not helpful unless heart failure is suspected
Not helpful unless acute coronary syndrome is suspected

decision_points: Always check point-of-care glucose early; hypoglycemia is rapidly reversible
Pregnancy test before imaging with ionizing radiation in anyone who could be pregnant
If focal deficits or recent fall, CT head before assuming metabolic cause
If fever and neck stiffness, lumbar puncture after appropriate imaging

criteria.name: DSM-5 delirium criteria (paraphrased)
criteria.summary: Delirium is diagnosed clinically when there is a disturbance in attention and awareness that develops acutely and fluctuates, plus another cognitive disturbance, not better explained by a pre-existing neurocognitive disorder, and evidence that the disturbance is caused by a medical condition, substance, or medication.

differential.name: Dementia
differential.why_considered: Chronic confusion and memory loss may be mistaken for delirium, especially in older adults.

history: Gradual onset over months to years
Memory loss is usually the first and most prominent symptom
Stable or slowly progressive course without acute fluctuation
Attention and alertness are preserved until later stages
exam: Alert and attentive on mental status testing
Deficits in memory and executive function but not fluctuating attention
labs: No acute metabolic derangements to explain cognitive decline
imaging: Cortical atrophy, ventricular enlargement, or chronic vascular changes
No acute hemorrhage, infarct, or mass

differential.name: Acute stroke
differential.why_considered: Sudden-onset confusion or altered mental status can be caused by a stroke, especially in older adults with vascular risk factors.
differential.trigger: Sudden focal neurologic deficit or high vascular risk

history: Sudden onset of focal weakness, numbness, or language difficulty
Maximal deficit at onset rather than fluctuating
Vascular risk factors: hypertension, atrial fibrillation, prior stroke
exam: Focal findings such as hemiparesis, facial droop, aphasia, dysarthria, or gaze deviation
Neglect syndrome or visual field cut
labs: Coagulation studies may be abnormal if on anticoagulants
imaging: CT head without contrast shows acute hemorrhage or early ischemic signs
MRI brain shows acute ischemic diffusion restriction
ecg: Atrial fibrillation may suggest cardioembolic source

differential.name: Nonconvulsive status epilepticus
differential.why_considered: Altered awareness with a fluctuating course can be nonconvulsive seizure activity rather than delirium.
differential.trigger: Known seizure disorder, recent seizure, or unexplained fluctuating consciousness

history: Known epilepsy
Recent witnessed convulsion
Subtle motor signs such as lip smacking or eye blinking
Postictal confusion after a seizure
exam: Automatisms, eyelid fluttering, or gaze deviation
In postictal state: transient focal weakness and gradually improving mental status
labs: Prolactin may be elevated after generalized seizure but is not reliable
imaging: CT or MRI may show a structural lesion such as old stroke, tumor, or mesial temporal sclerosis

differential.name: Hypoglycemia
differential.why_considered: Hypoglycemia is a common, rapidly reversible cause of altered mental status that can mimic delirium.
differential.trigger: Diabetes treated with insulin or sulfonylureas, or any patient with altered mental status

history: Diabetes on insulin or sulfonylurea
Symptoms may include sweating, tremor, palpitations, or hunger preceding confusion
Recent missed meal, increased activity, or alcohol use
exam: Often stuporous but may be agitated
labs: Point-of-care glucose < 70 mg/dL, often much lower

differential.name: Acute psychosis
differential.why_considered: Hallucinations and delusions can be features of delirium, but may be a primary psychiatric disorder.

history: Prior psychiatric diagnosis
Auditory hallucinations more common than visual
Clear sensorium and oriented to person, place, and time
Chronic or subacute course without acute medical illness
exam: No fluctuation in level of consciousness
labs: No acute metabolic or infectious precipitant

differential.name: Depression
differential.why_considered: Hypoactive delirium with withdrawal and lethargy may look like depression, especially in older adults.

history: Gradual onset of low mood over weeks
No acute change in attention or alertness
Vegetative symptoms: poor sleep, poor appetite, low energy
No medical precipitant
exam: Attention may be reduced due to poor motivation but can be redirected
Psychomotor slowing but no acute medical signs

severity.mild: Mild inattention, restlessness, and disorientation; patient is alert and cooperative, with no danger to self or others, and symptoms fluctuate.
severity.moderate: Fluctuating confusion with either agitation or somnolence; patient may pick at lines or need repeated redirection, but responds to verbal cues and maintains airway.
severity.severe: Marked agitation with pulling at tubes or severe somnolence requiring frequent stimulation; may have hallucinations, delusions, or threaten self-harm; needs frequent observation.
severity.critical: Stuporous or comatose, or severe hyperactive delirium with autonomic instability (hypertension, tachycardia, hyperthermia); may be life-threatening and requires emergency sedation and airway management.

red_flags.meaning: Possible stroke or structural brain lesion; urgent brain imaging.

red_flags.finding: Fever with neck stiffness or photophobia
red_flags.meaning: Meningitis or encephalitis until proven otherwise.
Pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, or hypoventilation may be precipitating; treat immediately.

red_flags.finding: Autonomic instability with high fever and rigidity
red_flags.meaning: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome, serotonin syndrome, or severe withdrawal; immediate medical treatment.
Medication-induced delirium or withdrawal; review and adjust medications.

red_flags.finding: Seizure activity or prolonged postictal state
red_flags.meaning: Nonconvulsive status epilepticus; consider EEG and antiepileptics.

complications.name: Falls with injury
clues: Agitation and attempts to get out of bed

complications.name: Persistent cognitive impairment
clues: Prolonged delirium lasting days to weeks

special_populations.differences: Hypoactive delirium predominates and is often mistaken for depression or worsening dementia; higher risk of falls, aspiration, and persistent cognitive decline.

May present with irritability, inconsolable crying, or emergence agitation after anesthesia; young children cannot describe confusion, and disorientation is less obvious; underlying infection or medication is common.
Delirium is rare; consider eclampsia, infection, or medication effects; avoid unnecessary restraints and use the least harmful imaging.
Higher risk of CNS infection or medication toxicity; lower threshold for lumbar puncture and broader workup.

key_questions.question: When did the confusion start?
key_questions.looking_for: Acute onset over hours to days, not gradual decline over months

key_questions.question: Does the confusion come and go, and is it worse at night?
key_questions.looking_for: Fluctuating course with periods of lucidity; often worse in the evening

key_questions.question: Have you had trouble paying attention or following what is being said?
key_questions.looking_for: Inattention: cannot stay focused, loses track of questions

key_questions.question: Have you been seeing or hearing things that are not there?
key_questions.looking_for: Visual hallucinations or illusions, especially at night

key_questions.question: What medicines have you started or changed recently, including over-the-counter, sleep aids, or pain medicines?
key_questions.looking_for: New or increased sedating, opioid, anticholinergic, or steroid agent

key_questions.question: Have you had fever, chills, cough, or burning with urination?
key_questions.looking_for: Signs of pneumonia or urinary tract infection

key_questions.question: Do you use alcohol or any drugs? When was your last drink or use?
key_questions.looking_for: Alcohol or drug intoxication or withdrawal

key_questions.question: What is the patient's usual memory and day-to-day functioning? Is there known dementia?
key_questions.looking_for: Baseline cognitive status; delirium is an acute change from baseline

key_questions.question: Any recent falls or hit to the head?
key_questions.looking_for: Possible subdural hematoma or traumatic brain injury

key_questions.question: Any weakness, numbness, trouble speaking, or facial droop?
key_questions.looking_for: Focal neurologic deficit suggesting stroke or structural lesion

key_questions.question: Any fever with headache and stiff neck?
key_questions.looking_for: Meningitis or encephalitis until proven otherwise

reasoning_points: Acute confusion with inattention and disorientation that fluctuates over hours and is worse at night
A precipitating medical problem, medication, or withdrawal is identified or suspected
Medication review reveals a new or increased sedating, opioid, or anticholinergic agent
No focal neurologic deficit or meningeal signs, making structural or infectious CNS lesion less likely, though imaging and CSF are considered if indicated
The course differs from dementia: acute onset and fluctuating attention rather than gradual memory decline
Common reversible causes such as hypoglycemia, infection, hypoxia, and electrolyte disturbance are addressed early

easy: Older adult who is hospitalized or post-operative
Hypoactive subtype: sleepy, withdrawn, and inattentive
Obvious precipitant, such as a urinary tract infection
Classic fluctuating course with worsening at night
No focal neurologic findings or meningeal signs
medium: Hyperactive delirium with agitation and visual hallucinations, resembling primary psychosis
Medication-induced, such as benzodiazepine, opioid, or anticholinergic
Delirium superimposed on dementia, making the acute change harder to recognize
Multiple potential contributing factors but no single obvious cause
hard: Nonconvulsive status epilepticus presenting as fluctuating confusion
Delirium with focal neurologic signs requiring urgent stroke workup
Intensive care unit delirium with multiple contributors, sedation, and coma
Alcohol withdrawal or delirium tremens with autonomic instability
No obvious precipitant and normal initial labs, prompting broader metabolic and neurologic evaluation
